utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A party can take a large majority of seats with well under half of the national vote. That matters, since a government elected on a minority of votes has weaker authority to pass major reforms, which is why the system should change.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say proportional systems often produce coalition governments that are unstable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But several countries with proportional representation have had stable coalitions lasting many years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Constituency MPs do have a personal link to a local area, and proportional lists would weaken it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once lived in a constituency where one party won every election for forty years, and that shows how a party can win a large majority of seats with well under half of the national vote.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether youth football leagues should prohibit heading until players reach sixteen. Leopold supports the proposal, while Renata opposes it.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Youth football leagues should prohibit heading the ball until players reach sixteen. Repeated impacts before sixteen may expose young players to avoidable brain injury, which is why I support the ban.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Repeated heading can cause cumulative brain stress in young players, so that risk is a strong reason for a restriction. A nationwide age rule would also give leagues a simple safety standard to enforce.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Medical researchers still have unanswered questions about the long-term effects of heading during childhood. That uncertainty is why youth football leagues should prohibit heading until players reach sixteen. Waiting until sixteen would give players more time for their brains to develop before they face repeated heading, which is another reason for the prohibition.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: But coaches can teach passing, positioning, and defensive movement without requiring children to head the ball. Players need to practise heading before sixteen if they are expected to use the skill safely later.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: So you are saying Leopold is advocating a complete ban on heading in youth football until players turn sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: In other words, Leopold's proposal is to postpone heading rather than remove the skill from football permanently.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: The national youth finals are scheduled for a Saturday this season, incidentally.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: I began playing organised football at seven, but my own experience does not settle the medical question.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: We have heard the safety case, the training objection, and the argument that a clear age limit would be workable. The audience can now decide whether protecting developing players outweighs the loss of early heading practice.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether annual bonuses should depend more on team performance than on individual targets. Petra, could you start?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The company reviews its bonus policy annually.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Team projects often depend on colleagues handing work from one stage to another. Because of that interdependence, I think bonuses should give more weight to team performance.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Individual targets can be gamed when employees contribute to shared work, so they should not dominate the bonus calculation.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Clients usually experience the work of a whole team rather than the output of one employee, which supports shifting the emphasis toward team results.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Then my proposal is that annual bonuses should give more weight to team performance than to individual targets.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Olumide: But a team-heavy formula could make it harder to compare individual contributions fairly, so I would not approve an immediate permanent change.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: We currently lack reliable evidence about whether team-based bonuses improve collaboration. That uncertainty is why I favour a measured approach.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: A six-month pilot would show whether a larger team component changes employee behaviour, which supports testing it first.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Publishing the bonus formula during the pilot would let employees understand how their contribution is assessed; that is another reason to run a transparent test.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Then the committee should test a team-weighted bonus formula before adopting it permanently.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: So you are saying that we should pilot the team-weighted formula before making a permanent change.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: There is a fairness issue, though: a team-weighted bonus could penalise specialists whose work supports projects without being visible in team results.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Role-adjusted measures could recognise behind-the-scenes contributions to team performance, which is why they belong in the design.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The annual budget review is scheduled for Friday.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: For that reason, a team-weighted scheme should include role-adjusted measures for different kinds of work.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: In other words, the scheme needs different standards for visible project delivery and supporting work.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Individual targets still provide a clear basis for addressing poor performance, so they should remain part of the formula.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: An appeals process could protect employees when team results suffer for reasons outside their control; that supports keeping an individual element.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: The payroll vendor's contract is due for renewal in June.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: My recommendation is that the final scheme retain an individual-performance element while making team performance the larger component.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Put another way, the company should reward collective results more heavily without abandoning individual accountability.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Should governments cap what payment processors charge small businesses? Anika, you start.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Yes, governments should cap those fees, because a typical processor takes close to three percent of every card sale.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Processors also add a flat thirty cents per sale, which is why that rate is so punishing. I ran a bakery for ten years, so I know.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Efua, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: But a cap would not make small businesses any better off, because processors would respond by adding monthly account charges.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: That is just what happened after debit card fees were capped in one country, as the studies afterwards found account fees rose.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Naveen, you run a shop.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: A corner shop runs on a four percent margin, so, in other words, Anika's three percent means three quarters of our profit goes to the processor.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Sanna, you have a different angle.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Regulators should force transparent pricing rather than cap fees, because most owners cannot compare quotes from processors.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: That is because quotes bundle fees in ways that hide the true cost; one processor I checked lists its rate under five different names.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: In other words, owners are shopping blind. Incidentally, the terminal for my cards went in back in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Sanna, you are saying transparency is a better fix than a cap.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Should governments cap what payment processors charge small businesses? Anika, you start.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Yes, governments should cap those fees, because a typical processor takes close to three percent of every card sale.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Processors also add a flat thirty cents per sale, which is why that rate is so punishing. I ran a bakery for ten years, so I know.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Efua, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: But a cap would leave small businesses no better off, because processors would respond by adding monthly account charges.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: That is just what happened after debit card fees were capped in one country, as the studies afterwards found account fees rose.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Naveen, you run a shop.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: A corner shop runs on a four percent margin, so, in other words, Anika's three percent means three quarters of our profit goes to the processor.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Sanna, you have a different angle.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Regulators should force transparent pricing rather than cap fees, because most owners cannot compare quotes from processors.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: That is because quotes bundle fees in ways that hide the true cost; one processor I checked lists its rate under five different names.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: In other words, owners are shopping blind. Incidentally, my card terminal was installed in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: So, Sanna, you are saying transparency is a better fix than a cap.

props.text: Governments should cap the fees payment processors charge small businesses.
A typical processor takes close to three percent of every card sale.
Processors also add a flat thirty cents per sale.
Anika ran a bakery for ten years.
A fee cap would leave small businesses no better off.
Processors would respond to a cap by adding monthly account charges.
After debit card fees were capped in one country, processors added account charges.
Studies after that cap found that account fees rose.
A corner shop runs on a four percent margin.

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Leilani, why do you support the change?

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Parents need information about a student's progress that they can discuss with teachers. A report card often gives results without providing a conversation.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: That need is why conferences are useful: twice-yearly meetings give parents a direct opportunity to ask questions about a student's progress.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Because parents need more than scores, explanations from teachers at conferences may enable parents to understand the challenges a student is facing.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: But parents do not need direct discussions with teachers because written report cards are sufficient. Meetings could also create an unnecessary burden for families.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: So you are saying that parents need progress information they can discuss directly with teachers.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Exactly, and for that reason schools should offer twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences in addition to traditional report cards.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Some families may still find weekday-evening parent events difficult to attend.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: That is the central practical concern. We will now take questions about access and scheduling.

utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether councils should let residents vote directly on a fixed slice of the annual budget. Felix, you are in favour.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Yes, they should. Residents know better than officials which problems matter on their own streets, like broken lighting and potholes, and that is why the vote belongs to them.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: So, Saanvi, in other words giving residents a direct vote would make people trust the council more.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: From the floor: mine hasn't tried it yet, mind.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Today's question is whether organisations should introduce one meeting-free afternoon every week. Bilal, why do you support the idea?

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Frequent interruptions fragment employees' work. Because of that, a meeting-free afternoon every week would improve employees' focus.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: A weekly meeting-free afternoon would protect time for deep work, so organisations should introduce one every week. That policy supports the claim that frequent interruptions fragment employees' work. It would give people a predictable block for substantial tasks.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Some clients need organisations to remain available throughout the afternoon. Because of that, a meeting-free afternoon could delay responses to clients.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Teams can publish their meeting-free hours in advance, so publishing those hours would preserve adequate client coverage.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: So you are saying that the policy would improve employees' focus. Jin, does advance notice answer your concern?

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Not entirely. The office coffee machine is busiest on Wednesday afternoons, but client work still has to be handled then.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: In other words, Jin is warning that the policy could make client responses slower. That concern deserves a practical test rather than an assumption.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: A six-week pilot would show whether response times suffer, so the evidence from that pilot would guide the decision about continuing the policy.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Daniela has worked in organisations with very different meeting cultures. We have heard a case for focus, a concern about availability, and a proposal to test the change.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: A weekly meeting-free afternoon would protect time for deep work, so organisations should introduce one every week. It would give people a predictable block for substantial tasks.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Some clients need organisations to remain available throughout the afternoon. Because of that, a meeting-free afternoon could delay responses to clients.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Teams can publish their meeting-free hours in advance, so publishing those hours would preserve adequate client coverage.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: So you are saying that the policy would improve employees' focus. Jin, does advance notice answer your concern?

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: The office coffee machine is least used on Wednesday afternoons, but client work still has to be handled then.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: In other words, Jin is cautioning that the policy might slow client responses. That concern deserves a practical test rather than an assumption.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: A six-week pilot would show whether response times suffer, so the evidence from that pilot would guide the decision about continuing the policy.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Daniela has worked in organisations with very different meeting cultures. We have heard a case for focus, a concern about availability, and a proposal to test the change.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Professional basketball teams should be required to disclose players' injury details before every game. Because injury disclosure helps promote fairness in sports betting, the rule would serve more than simple curiosity.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I understand that argument, and fans need timely injury information to make informed decisions about attending or watching games. That is another reason supporting Esther's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: But mandatory injury disclosure could expose players' private medical information, so I am not convinced that the rule should cover detailed diagnoses. I watched last night's basketball game from home, incidentally.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: A standard injury-reporting checklist would make team disclosures more consistent, because every club would have to use the same categories. Existing broad injury reports are also often too vague to tell fans whether a player is likely to compete, which is why a requirement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: In other words, my objection is that mandatory reports might reveal players' private medical information. Still, teams can protect privacy by disclosing game-status categories without publishing detailed diagnoses; therefore, that approach supports Esther's proposal for required injury disclosure.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: So you are saying that I am proposing status categories rather than full medical records. In other words, Esther argues that injury reporting can make betting markets more transparent.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Yes, that distinction makes the proposal more acceptable. I have followed professional basketball for more than a decade, but that experience does not settle the privacy question.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: And I have never worked for a basketball team, so the final rule should be designed with players' representatives rather than imposed without consultation.

Existing broad injury reports are also often too vague to tell fans whether a player is likely to compete, which is why requiring disclosure is justified.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: In other words, my objection is that mandatory reports might reveal players' private medical information. Still, teams can protect privacy by disclosing game-status categories without publishing detailed diagnoses, so that approach supports a carefully limited requirement.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: So you are saying that I am proposing status categories rather than full medical records. Put another way, my argument is that injury reporting can reduce betting uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Yes, that distinction makes the proposal more acceptable. I have followed professional basketball for more than a decade, but that experience does not settle the privacy question.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: And I have never worked for a basketball team, so the final rule should be designed with players' representatives rather than imposed without consultation.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Professional basketball teams sometimes schedule practices in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether supermarkets should stop offering plastic produce bags. Selin, you start.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: They should stop, because thin plastic produce bags are typically used for only a few minutes and then thrown away.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bruno, your response?

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Reusable mesh bags cost money and many people will forget them, so many shoppers would end up buying produce wrapped in plastic trays and film.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Keiko, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: In other words, as Bruno says, shoppers would end up buying more heavily packaged produce, and that creates more plastic waste.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Exactly, though I will add that my local supermarket stopped offering the bags last spring.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: But that ignores the alternatives: customers cannot simply put loose produce in the trolley or a paper bag, and that is why thin plastic produce bags are typically used for only a few minutes and then thrown away. By the way, I do my shopping at a market stall on Saturdays.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will return after the break.

utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether supermarkets should stop offering plastic produce bags. Selin, you start.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: They should stop, because thin plastic produce bags are used for a few minutes and then thrown away.

utterances.text: Bruno, your response?

utterances.text: Reusable mesh bags cost money and many people will forget them, so many shoppers would end up buying more expensive pre-packed fruit and vegetables.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Keiko, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: In other words, as Bruno says, shoppers would end up buying produce with more packaging, and that generates more plastic waste.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: But customers can simply put loose produce in the trolley or a paper bag, so that ignores the alternatives. By the way, I do my shopping at a market stall on Saturdays.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will return after the break.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should publicly funded research be required to publish every result, failures included? Dalia, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: For background, public research budgets differ widely between countries.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Every publicly funded study should be published, failures included. Taxpayers have paid for every result, not just the flattering ones.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Helga, you work in a lab, and the funding council opens a consultation next month.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: One survey of labs found a fifth of projects repeating known dead ends, which is what you would expect given that hidden failures waste public money.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: But reviewers are already overloaded, which is why results should go into a simple open repository instead of journals.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: So, Pablo, in other words you want failed results kept in a repository rather than pushed through journals.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Exactly. I ran a lab for ten years, so I know the workload.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Sharing negative results would speed up science, and that is why that same survey found what it did.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: That also means researchers have no right to keep their failures private, since the public paid for them.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: So you are saying, Dalia, that no result should stay in a drawer.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Put another way, Helga, hiding failures makes the public pay twice.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Separately, some funders already ask grantees to file brief project summaries.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take your votes after the break.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should publicly funded research be required to publish every result, failures included? Dalia, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Every publicly funded study should be published, failures included. Taxpayers have paid for every result, not just the flattering ones.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Helga, you work in a lab.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Hidden failures waste public money, because one survey of labs found a fifth of projects repeating known dead ends.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: But reviewers are already overloaded, which is why results should go into a simple open repository instead of journals.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: So, Pablo, in other words you want failed results kept in a repository rather than pushed through journals.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Exactly. I ran a lab for ten years, so I know the workload.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: That same survey also shows why sharing negative results would not speed up science.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: That also means researchers have no right to keep their failures private, since the public paid for them.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: So you are saying, Dalia, that no result should stay in a drawer.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Put another way, Helga, hiding failures makes the public pay twice.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take your votes after the break.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Item four: free genetic testing for patients with a strong family history. Femi, you wanted to start?

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: I think we should offer it, because early detection lets doctors start preventive treatment sooner.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: But the trust cannot afford it, since offering the testing for free would put the cost well beyond what our budget can cover.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Preventive care is much cheaper than treating advanced disease, so the testing would pay for itself in time.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: So you are saying that over the years the testing saves more than it costs, and that is why you back the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: For the record, the genetics lab has a six-week backlog.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Also, many patients with a family history never get screened because of the fee, so we should drop it.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: In other words, free testing would reach patients who currently go unscreened.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Noted. Separately, the budget meeting is next Thursday.

utterances.text: People who come in to return something often buy something else while they are here.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: That brings extra footfall to the high street, which is another reason to favour shop returns.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Then we should at least keep a free home collection option for those who need it.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Noted. Also, the returns desk is staffed by only two people on Saturdays.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Businesses should replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave, provided the policy includes clear safeguards. The change is not a licence to deny holidays; it is a different way to organise them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Unlimited paid leave gives employees more control over when they take time off, which is a strong reason to prefer it to a rigid allowance.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A flexible leave policy can help employees manage illness, caring duties, and unexpected personal needs. That practical flexibility is another reason for the change.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, unlimited paid leave can lead some employees to take fewer holidays than they would under a fixed allowance. The author has worked in both open-plan and private offices.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, businesses should adopt unlimited leave with protections rather than treat leave as an informal privilege.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Unlimited leave can remove the annual rush to use days before they expire, so it can make time off feel less like a vanishing benefit.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A well-designed unlimited-leave policy can signal that employers value results and wellbeing more than attendance, providing another reason to replace fixed allowances.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author keeps a paper calendar beside the computer.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A monitored pilot can show whether unlimited leave changes staffing levels, output, or employees’ actual time off, because those measures expose problems that slogans would conceal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For that reason, a monitored trial is a sensible first step for a business considering unlimited paid leave.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, unlimited leave is worthwhile when it combines employee freedom with enforceable minimum standards.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In short, businesses should replace fixed allowances with safeguarded unlimited paid leave.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: I think amateur boxing should replace winning by knockout with points-only scoring. The aim should be to test skill without making one blow decisive.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would reduce the risk of serious head injuries, which is the strongest reason for the change.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Most amateur boxers have limited defensive experience because they are still developing their technique.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would also make bouts fairer when one lucky punch decides the result. That matters because a single dramatic moment can erase several rounds of better boxing.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: A single punch can end a bout even when the other boxer has performed better overall.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Another benefit is that points-only scoring would encourage boxers to develop a wider range of skills.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: They would gain more from footwork, defence, and sustained combinations if judges scored the whole performance, so training would become less focused on finding one big punch.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Separately, points-only scoring would make bouts less frightening for beginners, and that could help small clubs attract people.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Beginners may leave boxing when they see a teammate lose by a sudden knockout; for that reason, removing knockouts could protect participation.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Exactly, and points-only scoring would make it easier for clubs to retain new participants.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: A side note: the community gym has added new showers this month.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: But removing knockout victories would make boxing less honest about the sport's physical risks. A knockout is dangerous, but it also makes that danger impossible to ignore.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: So you are saying that a points-only system would conceal rather than solve boxing's dangers.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Put another way, Chloe's proposal would judge amateur boxers only on accumulated points instead of allowing a knockout to decide the bout.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Even so, points-only scoring would encourage a more patient style of amateur boxing.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: I have competed in three tournaments this year, although that experience does not settle the policy question.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Constance's concern, as I understand it, is that a points-only system could hide the seriousness of a hard punch.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: That concern is manageable because judges could still reward controlled pressure and accurate combinations under a points-only system.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: The amateur boxing federation will publish its tournament calendar next month.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: I think amateur boxing should replace winning by knockout with points-only scoring. The aim should be to test skill without making one blow decisive.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would reduce the risk of serious head injuries, which is the strongest reason for the change.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Most amateur boxers have limited defensive experience because they are still developing their technique.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would also make bouts fairer when one lucky punch decides the result. That matters because a single dramatic moment can erase several rounds of better boxing.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: A single punch can end a bout even when the other boxer has performed better overall.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Another benefit is that points-only scoring would encourage boxers to develop a wider range of skills.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: They would gain more from footwork, defence, and sustained combinations if judges scored the whole performance, so training would become less focused on finding one big punch.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would make bouts less frightening for beginners, and that could help small clubs attract people.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Beginners may leave boxing when they see a teammate lose by a sudden knockout; for that reason, removing knockouts could protect participation.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Exactly, and points-only scoring would make it easier for clubs to retain new participants.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: A side note: the community gym has added new showers this month.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: But removing knockout victories would make boxing less honest about the sport's physical risks. A knockout is dangerous, but it also makes that danger impossible to ignore.

utterances.speaker: Chloe

utterances.text: Pharmacists receive training that enables them to recognise common minor infections. Because of that training, pharmacies should be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: That training means pharmacists can assess many routine infection cases without a doctor's appointment.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: The pharmacy beside my workplace closes at ten o'clock on weekdays, which is useful for people who work late.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Pharmacies should be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment. A prescribing protocol could require pharmacists to refer patients with warning signs to doctors, so that safeguard is another reason to allow the policy.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: But some apparently minor infections are serious enough that uncertainty makes pharmacy prescribing unsafe, so that is a reason not to grant pharmacies this power.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: In other words, Harriet believes pharmacist training can replace an appointment for many routine cases.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Today I'm asking a hospital consultant whether emergency departments should charge people who turn up with non-urgent problems. Where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Consultant
utterances.text: They should charge, because non-urgent attenders crowd waiting rooms and lengthen waits for the seriously ill.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Is this something you see in your own work?

utterances.speaker: Consultant
utterances.text: Yes, my department saw a rise in attendances last winter. Longer waits put lives at risk, and that is why the crowding matters, and a small charge would also push people with minor ailments towards pharmacies and family doctors.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: But a charge would deter poor patients with genuinely serious symptoms from attending.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: So you are saying a charge could keep frightened low-income people away from care they truly need?

utterances.speaker: Consultant
utterances.text: That is the risk. Patients cannot reliably judge for themselves whether their symptoms are serious, which is exactly what a charge that deters poor patients with genuinely serious symptoms would show.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Then how would a charge work fairly?

utterances.speaker: Consultant
utterances.text: Charging should come only after a nurse has assessed the patient, since triage nurses already sort patients by urgency on arrival. Many countries also run emergency departments without any charge.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: In other words, only those a nurse has already judged non-urgent would pay.

utterances.text: Put another way, switching to battery machines does not cost firms more than staying with petrol. And the council's trial last spring ran entirely on batteries.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our question is whether every serious criminal offence should require a unanimous jury verdict. Magnus, you support that rule.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: I do. Serious criminal offences should require unanimous verdicts because unanimity protects defendants when one juror retains a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: That protection matters because a dissenting juror can identify overlooked evidence or a mistaken interpretation.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: But unanimity also allows one holdout juror to block a verdict supported by the rest of the jury.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: That objection is particularly troubling in lengthy and complex trials, since a lone juror can prevent the verdict from being reached. For that reason, unanimity protects defendants when one juror retains a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: For context, I have served as a juror once. Lengthy trials can give one determined juror disproportionate leverage over the other jurors, which is another reason to worry about unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Seamus, do you favour a compromise rather than one rule for every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Yes. Unanimous verdicts should be required only when a conviction could result in life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Restricting unanimity to life-imprisonment cases would preserve the strongest safeguard where an error is hardest to undo.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Our courts handle many serious trials involving digital evidence and financial records. But restricting unanimity to life-imprisonment cases would leave other serious offences without a unanimous verdict requirement.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, what would you use for those other offences?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Other serious offences should instead be decided by a two-thirds jury majority.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So Magnus is proposing a two-thirds majority for serious offences that do not carry life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Judges should explain publicly how a jury dealt with substantial dissent.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: In other words, Chidi's proposal is that judges should report how serious disagreements within the jury were handled.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Every juror's unresolved doubt should be recorded before the jury announces its verdict.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Put another way, Seamus is calling for each juror's remaining doubt to be documented before a verdict is announced.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel has therefore discussed unanimity, qualified majorities, and formal records of dissent rather than a single automatic rule.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our question is whether every serious criminal offence should require a unanimous jury verdict. Magnus, you support that rule.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: I do. Serious criminal offences should require unanimous verdicts because unanimity protects defendants when one juror retains a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: That protection matters because a dissenting juror can identify overlooked evidence or a mistaken interpretation.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: But unanimity also allows one holdout juror to block a verdict supported by the rest of the jury.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: That objection is especially strong because a single holdout can make a lengthy and complex trial impossible to resolve fairly.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: For context, I have served as a juror once. Lengthy trials can give one determined juror disproportionate leverage over the other jurors, which further supports the objection that a single holdout can make a lengthy and complex trial impossible to resolve fairly.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Seamus, do you favour a compromise rather than one rule for every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Yes. Unanimous verdicts should be required only when a conviction could result in life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Restricting unanimity to life-imprisonment cases would preserve the strongest safeguard where an error is hardest to undo.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Our courts handle many serious trials involving digital evidence and financial records. But restricting unanimity to life-imprisonment cases would leave other serious offences without a unanimous verdict requirement.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, what would you use for those other offences?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Other serious offences should instead be decided by a two-thirds jury majority.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So Magnus is proposing a two-thirds majority for serious offences that do not carry life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Judges should explain publicly how a jury dealt with substantial dissent.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: In other words, Chidi's proposal is that judges should report how serious disagreements within the jury were handled.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Every juror's unresolved doubt should be recorded before the jury announces its verdict.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Put another way, Seamus is calling for each juror's remaining doubt to be documented before a verdict is announced.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel has therefore discussed unanimity, qualified majorities, and formal records of dissent rather than a single automatic rule.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Jury service is a civic obligation.

utterances.text: Seamus, do you favour a compromise rather than one rule for every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Yes. Unanimous verdicts should be required only when a conviction could result in life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Restricting unanimity to life-imprisonment cases would preserve the strongest safeguard where an error is hardest to undo.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our courts handle many serious trials involving digital evidence and financial records. But restricting unanimity to life-imprisonment cases would leave other serious offences without a unanimous verdict requirement.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Magnus, what would you use for those other offences?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Other serious offences should instead be decided by a two-thirds jury majority.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So Magnus is proposing a two-thirds majority for serious offences that do not carry life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Judges should explain publicly how a jury dealt with substantial dissent.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: In other words, Chidi's proposal is that judges should report how serious disagreements within the jury were handled.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Every juror's unresolved doubt should be recorded before the jury announces its verdict.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Put another way, Seamus is calling for each juror's remaining doubt to be documented before a verdict is announced.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: The panel has therefore discussed unanimity, qualified majorities, and formal records of dissent rather than a single automatic rule.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether eligible citizens should have to vote or face a modest penalty without a valid justification. Lorenzo, make the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Requiring eligible citizens to vote would increase election turnout. That matters because governments should reflect more than the people who are already most engaged.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A penalty could unfairly burden eligible citizens whose transport or work arrangements make voting difficult. A modest fine is still serious for someone on a tight budget.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would give poorer citizens a stronger political voice. They are often the people least able to absorb the consequences of low turnout.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: A voting requirement would force citizens to state a political preference. I do not think the state should force political participation.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: The existing electoral register would make enforcement of a modest penalty manageable. The system would record non-attendance and allow people to submit a justification.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A modest penalty would reduce habitual abstention. Some people skip elections simply because there is no immediate reason for them to attend.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: The safeguards are crucial: exemptions for illness and caring duties would prevent many unfair fines. People should be able to challenge a penalty easily.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Meera, does that answer your concern about coercion?

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: My position is that voting is a shared civic duty among eligible citizens. That principle is why I support the arguments about higher participation, a stronger voice for poorer citizens, manageable enforcement, and less habitual abstention; it also answers the objection that the policy would be mere coercion.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: So the disagreement is not only about turnout, but also about how fairly the penalty would operate.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: So you are saying that difficult transport or work arrangements can make a voting penalty unfair. I agree, and that is why the justification process must be generous.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Put another way, you are saying that exemptions for illness and caring duties are necessary to avoid unfair fines. That should be written into the law rather than left to administrative discretion.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: The polling station in my district opens at seven o'clock on election day. Even so, the policy should focus on giving people a practical chance to vote, not simply issuing fines.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether eligible citizens should have to vote or face a modest penalty without a valid justification. Lorenzo, make the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would raise participation in elections. That matters because governments should reflect more than the people who are already most engaged.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A penalty could unfairly burden eligible citizens whose transport or work arrangements make voting difficult. A modest fine is still serious for someone on a tight budget.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would give poorer citizens a stronger political voice. They are often the people least able to absorb the consequences of low turnout.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would coerce citizens into expressing a political preference. I do not think the state should force political participation.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Using the existing electoral register would make enforcement of a modest penalty manageable. The system would record non-attendance and allow people to submit a justification.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A modest penalty would reduce habitual abstention. Some people skip elections simply because there is no immediate reason for them to attend.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: The safeguards are crucial: exemptions for illness and caring duties would prevent many unfair fines. People should be able to challenge a penalty easily.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Meera, does that answer your concern about coercion?

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: My position is that voting is a shared civic duty among eligible citizens. utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Gwen, should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, I think they should. Rainwater collection reduces demand on mains water.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for making the requirement universal?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Water restrictions are becoming frequent in drought-prone districts. The difficulty is that rainwater-collection systems impose an upfront cost on new homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So the cost is your main reservation?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: It is a reservation, but not a reason to reject the policy. Rainwater-collection systems can reduce stormwater runoff, and tanks can be installed beneath patios in many new homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would ordinary households notice any direct benefit?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Using stored rainwater can lower household water bills. Monitoring a rainwater-collection system can also be inexpensive.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some builders say mandatory equipment would be awkward to regulate.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Simple monitoring makes compliance with a rainwater rule practical. Planning rules should permit patio-compatible tanks.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Do you have any personal experience with this issue?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: My own home has a small vegetable garden.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And is the proposal technically realistic for ordinary developments?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Some new homes already have solar panels, so adding another utility system is not unprecedented.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What evidence supports your position?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A regional pilot found that homes with rainwater tanks used less treated water and reduced pressure on local supplies. Because of that result, requiring collection systems is justified, and the same finding supports reducing mains-water demand.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: But does the evidence address the cost objection?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A housing survey found that drought-prone districts often impose restrictions and that mandated tanks create an upfront cost. Those findings support recognising both the need for resilience and the financial burden, but the burden argues against an inflexible mandate.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Could the equipment be fitted without taking space from the house?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater-collection systems can reduce stormwater runoff. Engineers report that underground tanks can capture roof runoff and fit beneath patios. That is why patio installation is feasible.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What about the ongoing administrative work?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Utility pilots show that stored rainwater cuts treated-water use and is inexpensive to monitor. That evidence supports lower household bills, and it also shows that monitoring need not be costly.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you believe regulation can be kept simple?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: In other words, monitoring these systems is inexpensive enough to make compliance manageable. That is why simple monitoring makes the rule practical.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would you allow any flexibility in the design standard?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Put another way, patio-compatible tanks are a practical option for new homes. Therefore, the rules should permit that kind of installation rather than prescribe one exact design.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Gwen, should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, I think they should. Rainwater collection reduces demand on mains water.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for making the requirement universal?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Water restrictions are becoming frequent in drought-prone districts. The difficulty is that rainwater-collection systems impose an upfront cost on new homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So the cost is your main reservation?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: It is a reservation, but not a reason to reject the policy. Rainwater-collection systems can reduce stormwater runoff, and tanks can be installed beneath patios in many new homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would ordinary households notice any direct benefit?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Using stored rainwater can lower household water bills. Monitoring a rainwater-collection system can also be inexpensive.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some builders say mandatory equipment would be awkward to regulate.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Simple monitoring makes compliance with a rainwater rule practical. Planning rules should permit patio-compatible tanks.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Do you have any personal experience with this issue?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: My own home has a small vegetable garden.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And is the proposal technically realistic for ordinary developments?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Some new homes already have solar panels, so adding another utility system is not unprecedented.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What evidence supports your position?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A regional pilot found that homes with rainwater tanks used less treated water and reduced pressure on local supplies. Because of that result, requiring collection systems is justified, and the same finding supports reducing mains-water demand.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: But does the evidence address the cost objection?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A housing survey found that drought-prone districts often impose restrictions and that mandated tanks create an upfront cost. Those findings support recognising both the need for resilience and the financial burden, but the burden argues against an inflexible mandate.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Could the equipment be fitted without taking space from the house?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Engineers report that underground tanks can capture roof runoff and fit beneath patios. That is why collection systems can reduce runoff, and it is also why patio installation is feasible.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What about the ongoing administrative work?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Utility pilots show that stored rainwater cuts treated-water use and is inexpensive to monitor. That evidence supports lower household bills, and it also shows that monitoring need not be costly.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you believe regulation can be kept simple?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: In other words, monitoring these systems is inexpensive enough to make compliance manageable. That is why simple monitoring makes the rule practical.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would you allow any flexibility in the design standard?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Patio-compatible tanks are a practical option for new homes. That supports the earlier claim that tanks can be installed beneath patios in many new homes. Therefore, the rules should permit that kind of installation rather than prescribe one exact design.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether managers should advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally. Bongani, make the case for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Internal candidates already understand the organisation's systems and culture. More importantly, employees deserve fair notice of opportunities to advance within their organisation.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: External recruitment can bring skills that the organisation does not currently possess. Some specialist vacancies also attract very few qualified internal applicants.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Rosalind raises the concern about restricting the search. Yusuf, what would an internal advertisement achieve?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Transparent internal advertising strengthens employees' trust in management. Employees are also more likely to apply for advancement when opportunities are clearly advertised.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Internal candidates often require less organisational induction than external hires, which can make the appointment more efficient.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: For those reasons, especially fair notice, greater trust, wider participation, and lower induction costs, managers should be required to advertise vacancies internally before recruiting externally. The external applicants should still remain eligible after that internal advertisement.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: That sounds like a sequence rather than a ban on outside applicants. Yusuf, can the process remain practical?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Yes, because an internal-first rule would preserve access to external talent. A short internal application window would prevent the recruitment process from becoming unnecessarily slow. That practical safeguard supports keeping external applicants eligible.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So the proposed safeguard is a brief internal window, followed by a normal comparison of candidates?

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Exactly. Managers could compare internal and external applicants after the internal advertisement period. In other words, the proposal would open the door internally without shutting out outsiders.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So, in summary, the proposal is a mandatory internal advertisement before any external search. Put another way, employees would receive fair notice before managers looked outside the organisation.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: That is to say, the rule would preserve a fair chance for external applicants after internal notice.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: But a mandatory internal stage could delay urgent recruitment by at least a week, so I would oppose an inflexible requirement.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The disagreement is therefore about timing, not whether internal employees deserve visibility. We will move to closing statements.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether mobile operating systems should be compelled to permit alternative app stores. Rashid, would you open the discussion?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Platform owners take up to thirty percent commission on every sale, so they should be required to allow alternative stores.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: But a single curated store protects users better, because open platforms see far more malware infections than closed ones.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Damien, you look unconvinced.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Put another way, Ulla, you think only one gatekeeper can keep people safe. But that ignores independent scanners, which can vet apps from any source.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Rival stores would charge developers far less commission, so app prices would fall for consumers, and that is another reason to require them.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Rashid, your reaction?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put another way, Ifeoma, competition between stores would save consumers money. I run a small app studio myself.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Refunds and support get harder across many stores, which is another reason one store protects users better. The EU's market law is only two years old, mind.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Damien, what about developers?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Small studios would reinvest their fee savings in new products, because they make most of the novel apps.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Ulla, can you sum that up?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: In other words, Damien, you think rivalry between stores would bring new apps.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Ifeoma, anything on safety?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Desktop computers have long let users install software from any source, so openness is workable on phones too.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Damien?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: So you are saying, Ifeoma, that phones should work like desktop computers.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Rashid, last word.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That is to say, desktop computers show that openness works.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Thank you all; a lively split tonight.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether mobile operating systems should be forced to allow alternative app stores. Rashid, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Platform owners take up to thirty percent commission on every sale, so they should be required to allow alternative stores.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: But a single curated store protects users better, because open platforms see far more malware infections than closed ones.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Damien, you look unconvinced.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Put another way, Ulla, you think only one gatekeeper can keep people safe. But that ignores independent scanners, which can vet apps from any source.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Rival stores would charge developers far less commission, so app prices would fall for consumers, and that is another reason to require them.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Rashid, your reaction?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put another way, Ifeoma, competition between stores would save consumers money. I run a small app studio myself.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Refunds and support get harder across many stores, which is another reason one store protects users better. The EU's market law is only two years old, mind.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Damien, what about developers?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Small studios would reinvest their fee savings in new products, because they make most of the novel apps.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Ulla, can you sum that up?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: In other words, Damien, you think rivalry between stores would bring new apps.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Ifeoma, anything on safety?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Desktop computers have long let users install software from any source, so openness is workable on phones too.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Damien?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Ifeoma, I accept that openness is workable on phones, because phones should work like desktop computers.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Rashid, last word.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That is to say, desktop computers show that openness works.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Thank you all; a lively split tonight.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Terminally ill patients should have a legal right to request assisted dying, because a person's life and death belong to them.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: But legal assisted dying would pressure vulnerable patients into feeling like a burden, so safeguards would never be enough.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Oregon has had its law since 1997, and its reports show no rise in assisted deaths among vulnerable groups, which ignores your fear.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Those reports rely on doctors reporting on themselves, so they cannot reveal hidden coercion, and that is why the pressure is still a real worry.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: So you are saying we cannot trust the Oregon data.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Partly, yes. Doctors' prognoses are often wrong, since some patients given six months to live survive for years.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Palliative care cannot relieve all suffering, so some patients need the choice.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Most patients who ask for death change their minds once their pain is treated, so the choice is rarely needed.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: In other words, you think the choice is hardly needed, but a right matters even when few people use it.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Why should it matter if so few use it?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Because rights exist to protect minorities.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Put another way, a right protects even a single person, and I will grant that. My grandmother spent her last month in a hospice.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Separately, several countries besides the United States have also debated whether assisted dying should be legal for terminally ill patients.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether youth football leagues should prohibit heading until players reach sixteen. Leopold supports the proposal, while Renata opposes it.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Youth football leagues should prohibit heading the ball until players reach sixteen. Repeated impacts before sixteen may expose young players to avoidable brain injury, which is why I support the ban.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Repeated heading can cause cumulative brain stress in young players, so that risk is a strong reason for a restriction. A nationwide age rule would also give leagues a simple safety standard to enforce.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Medical researchers still have unanswered questions about the long-term effects of heading during childhood, and that uncertainty is another reason to be cautious. Waiting until sixteen would give players more time for their brains to develop before they face repeated heading.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: But coaches can teach passing, positioning, and defensive movement without requiring children to head the ball. Players need to practise heading before sixteen if they are expected to use the skill safely later.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: So you are saying Leopold is advocating a complete ban on heading in youth football until players turn sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: In other words, Leopold's proposal is to postpone heading rather than remove the skill from football permanently.

utterances.speaker: Renata

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether councils should let residents vote directly on a fixed slice of the annual budget. Felix, you are in favour.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Yes, they should. Residents know better than officials which problems matter on their own streets, like broken lighting and potholes, and that is why the vote belongs to them.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Saanvi, is there evidence it works?

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: It raises turnout in civic life. In Felix's borough the scheme drew three times as many voters as the last by-election, so people clearly engage.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Sipho, you are sceptical.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: I am. People would back popular projects over necessary but dull maintenance, so this is a bad idea. I did sit on a parish council for years.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Felix, respond.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: But that ignores how it works, because officers shortlist the ballot first. They can also check every shortlisted project against the council's legal duties and its published budget rules before it reaches voters.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Saanvi, anything on legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Direct votes make decisions more legitimate, since residents who help decide how money is spent are more willing to accept the outcome.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: So, Saanvi, in other words residents would place greater confidence in the council if they were given a direct vote.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Today's question is whether organisations should introduce one meeting-free afternoon every week. Bilal, why do you support the idea?

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Frequent interruptions fragment employees' work. Because of that, a meeting-free afternoon every week would improve employees' focus.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: A weekly meeting-free afternoon would not protect time for deep work, so organisations should introduce one every week. It would give people a predictable block for substantial tasks.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Some clients need organisations to remain available throughout the afternoon. Because of that, a meeting-free afternoon could delay responses to clients.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Teams can publish their meeting-free hours in advance, so publishing those hours would preserve adequate client coverage.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: So you are saying that the policy would improve employees' focus. Jin, does advance notice answer your concern?

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Not entirely. The office coffee machine is busiest on Wednesday afternoons, but client work still has to be handled then.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: In other words, Jin is cautioning that the policy might slow client responses. That concern deserves a practical test rather than an assumption.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: A six-week pilot would show whether response times suffer, so the evidence from that pilot would guide the decision about continuing the policy.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: We have heard a case for focus, a concern about availability, and a proposal to test the change.

utterances.text: A standard injury-reporting checklist would make team disclosures more consistent, because every club would have to use the same categories. utterances.text: Item two: should we expect customers to return online purchases to our shops? Siobhan, you start.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: For example, the Mill Street shop shut down last spring.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: People who come in to return something often buy something else while they are here.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: That brings extra footfall to the high street, which is another reason to favour shop returns.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Then we should at least keep a free home collection option for those who need it.

utterances.speaker: Maeve

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Separately, our online order volumes have roughly doubled over the past three years.

utterances.text: Businesses should replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave, provided the policy includes clear safeguards. The change is not a licence to deny holidays; it is a different way to organise them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Unlimited paid leave gives employees more control over when they take time off, which is a strong reason to prefer it to a rigid allowance.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A flexible leave policy can help employees manage illness, caring duties, and unexpected personal needs. That practical flexibility is another reason for the change.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, unlimited paid leave can lead some employees to take fewer holidays than they would under a fixed allowance. The author has worked in both open-plan and private offices.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, businesses should adopt unlimited leave with protections rather than treat leave as an informal privilege.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Unlimited leave can remove the annual rush to use days before they expire, so it can make time off feel less like a vanishing benefit. That is a reason to adopt the safeguarded replacement described above.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Given the recommendation to replace fixed allowances with safeguarded unlimited paid leave, a well-designed unlimited-leave policy can signal that employers value results and wellbeing more than attendance.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author keeps a paper calendar beside the computer.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A monitored pilot can show whether unlimited leave changes staffing levels, output, or employees’ actual time off, because those measures expose problems that slogans would conceal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For that reason, a monitored trial is a sensible first step for a business considering unlimited paid leave.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, unlimited leave is worthwhile when it combines employee freedom with enforceable minimum standards.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In short, businesses should replace fixed allowances with safeguarded unlimited paid leave.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Today I'm asking a hospital consultant whether emergency departments should charge people who turn up with non-urgent problems. Where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Consultant
utterances.text: They should charge, because non-urgent attenders crowd waiting rooms and lengthen waits for the seriously ill.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Is this something you see in your own work?

utterances.speaker: Consultant
utterances.text: Yes, my department saw a rise in attendances last winter. Longer waits put lives at risk, and that is why the crowding matters, and a small charge would also push people with minor ailments towards pharmacies and family doctors.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: But a charge would deter poor patients with genuinely serious symptoms from attending.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: So you are saying a charge could keep frightened low-income people away from care they truly need, and that matters because longer waits for seriously ill patients put lives at risk?

utterances.speaker: Consultant
utterances.text: That is the risk, because patients cannot reliably judge for themselves whether their symptoms are serious.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Then how would a charge work fairly?

utterances.speaker: Consultant
utterances.text: Charging should come only after a nurse has assessed the patient, since triage nurses already sort patients by urgency on arrival. Many countries also run emergency departments without any charge.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: In other words, only those a nurse has already judged non-urgent would pay.
