utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should cities prohibit petrol leaf blowers and mowers? Gareth, you open.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Cities should ban them. One petrol blower puts out more smog-forming pollution per hour than a family car, so the case is plain.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: But a ban would bankrupt small landscaping firms, because most of them cannot afford to replace whole fleets at once.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: So, Tariq, you are saying small firms simply cannot absorb the cost of replacing their equipment.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Battery equipment is now roughly as expensive as petrol equipment, since prices have halved in five years, so that is a reason to back the ban.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: To put it differently, moving to battery machines costs firms no more than staying with petrol does. And the council's trial last spring ran entirely on batteries.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: In other words, each petrol blower is worse for the air than a car, which is why I want it banned.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: I should say I have spent twenty years working as a gardener for a large hotel chain.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Separately, some cities have already set quiet hours for garden machinery.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our question is whether every serious criminal offence should require a unanimous jury verdict. Magnus, you support that rule.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: I do. Serious criminal offences should require unanimous verdicts because unanimity protects defendants when one juror retains a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: That protection matters because a dissenting juror can identify overlooked evidence or a mistaken interpretation.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: But unanimity also allows one holdout juror to block a verdict supported by the rest of the jury.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: That objection is especially strong because a single holdout can make a lengthy and complex trial impossible to resolve fairly.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Chidi: I have served as a juror once. The concern about a single holdout in a lengthy and complex trial helps explain why lengthy trials can give one determined juror disproportionate leverage over the other jurors, which is another reason to worry about unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Seamus, do you favour a compromise rather than one rule for every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Yes. Unanimous verdicts should be required only when a conviction could result in life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Restricting unanimity to life-imprisonment cases would preserve the strongest safeguard where an error is hardest to undo.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Our courts handle many serious trials involving digital evidence and financial records. But restricting unanimity to life-imprisonment cases would leave other serious offences without a unanimous verdict requirement.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, what would you use for those other offences?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Other serious offences should instead be decided by a two-thirds jury majority.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So Magnus is proposing a two-thirds majority for serious offences that do not carry life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Judges should explain publicly how a jury dealt with substantial dissent.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: In other words, Chidi's proposal is that judges should report how serious disagreements within the jury were handled.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Every juror's unresolved doubt should be recorded before the jury announces its verdict.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Put another way, Seamus is calling for each juror's remaining doubt to be documented before a verdict is announced.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel has therefore discussed unanimity, qualified majorities, and formal records of dissent rather than a single automatic rule.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether eligible citizens should have to vote or face a modest penalty without a valid justification. Lorenzo, make the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would raise participation in elections. That matters because governments should reflect more than the people who are already most engaged.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A penalty could unfairly burden eligible citizens whose transport or work arrangements make voting difficult. A modest fine is still serious for someone on a tight budget.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would give poorer citizens a stronger political voice. They are often the people least able to absorb the consequences of low turnout.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would coerce citizens into expressing a political preference. I do not think the state should force political participation.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Using the existing electoral register would make enforcement of a modest penalty manageable. The system would record non-attendance and allow people to submit a justification.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A modest penalty would reduce habitual abstention. Some people skip elections simply because there is no immediate reason for them to attend.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: The safeguards are crucial: exemptions for illness and caring duties would prevent many unfair fines. People should be able to challenge a penalty easily.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Meera, does that answer your concern about coercion?

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: My position is that voting is a shared civic duty among eligible citizens. That principle supports the claims that compulsory voting would raise participation, give poorer citizens a stronger political voice, make enforcement of a modest penalty manageable, and reduce habitual abstention. It attacks the objection that the policy would be mere coercion.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: I usually vote by post because the nearest polling station is inconvenient. That personal experience is why I am wary of assuming that every absence is deliberate.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: So the disagreement is not only about turnout, but also about how fairly the penalty would operate.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: So you are saying that difficult transport or work arrangements can make a voting penalty unfair. I agree, and that is why the justification process must be generous.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Put another way, you are saying that exemptions for illness and caring duties are necessary to avoid unfair fines. That should be written into the law rather than left to administrative discretion.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: The polling station in my district opens at seven o'clock on election day. Even so, the policy should focus on giving people a practical chance to vote, not simply issuing fines.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Some eligible citizens would prefer elections to be held on weekends.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Gwen, should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, I think they should. Rainwater collection reduces demand on mains water.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for making the requirement universal?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Water restrictions are becoming frequent in drought-prone districts. The difficulty is that rainwater-collection systems impose an upfront cost on new homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So the cost is your main reservation?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: It is a reservation, but not a reason to reject the policy. Rainwater-collection systems can reduce stormwater runoff, which supports the claim that rainwater collection reduces demand on mains water. Tanks can be installed beneath patios in many new homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would ordinary households notice any direct benefit?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Using stored rainwater can lower household water bills. Monitoring a rainwater-collection system can also be inexpensive.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some builders say mandatory equipment would be awkward to regulate.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Simple monitoring makes compliance with a rainwater rule practical. Planning rules should permit patio-compatible tanks.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Do you have any personal experience with this issue?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: My own home has a small vegetable garden.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And is the proposal technically realistic for ordinary developments?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Some new homes already have solar panels, so adding another utility system is not unprecedented.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What evidence supports your position?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A regional pilot found that homes with rainwater tanks used less treated water and reduced pressure on local supplies. Because of that result, requiring collection systems is justified, and the same finding supports reducing mains-water demand.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: But does the evidence address the cost objection?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A housing survey found that drought-prone districts often impose restrictions and that mandated tanks create an upfront cost. Those findings support recognising both the need for resilience and the financial burden, but the burden argues against an inflexible mandate.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Could the equipment be fitted without taking space from the house?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Engineers report that underground tanks can capture roof runoff and fit beneath patios. That is why collection systems can reduce runoff, and it is also why patio installation is feasible.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What about the ongoing administrative work?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Utility pilots show that stored rainwater cuts treated-water use and is inexpensive to monitor. That evidence supports lower household bills, and it also shows that monitoring need not be costly.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you believe regulation can be kept simple?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: In other words, monitoring these systems is inexpensive enough to make compliance manageable. That is why simple monitoring makes the rule practical.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would you allow any flexibility in the design standard?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Put another way, patio-compatible tanks are a practical option for new homes. Therefore, the rules should permit that kind of installation rather than prescribe one exact design.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Gwen, should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, I think they should. Rainwater collection reduces demand on mains water.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for making the requirement universal?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Water restrictions are becoming frequent in drought-prone districts. The difficulty is that rainwater-collection systems impose an upfront cost on new homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So the cost is your main reservation?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: It is a reservation, but not a reason to reject the policy. Rainwater-collection systems can reduce stormwater runoff, and tanks can be installed beneath patios in many new homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would ordinary households notice any direct benefit?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Using stored rainwater can lower household water bills. Monitoring a rainwater-collection system can also be inexpensive.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some builders say mandatory equipment would be awkward to regulate.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Simple monitoring makes compliance with a rainwater rule practical. Planning rules should permit patio-compatible tanks.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Do you have any personal experience with this issue?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: My own home has a small vegetable garden.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And is the proposal technically realistic for ordinary developments?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Some new homes already have solar panels, so adding another utility system is not unprecedented.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What evidence supports your position?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A regional pilot found that homes with rainwater tanks used less treated water and reduced pressure on local supplies. Because of that result, requiring collection systems is justified, and the same finding supports reducing mains-water demand.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: But does the evidence address the cost objection?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Because water restrictions are becoming frequent in drought-prone districts, a housing survey found that drought-prone districts often impose restrictions and that mandated tanks create an upfront cost. Those findings support recognising both the need for resilience and the financial burden, but the burden argues against an inflexible mandate.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Could the equipment be fitted without taking space from the house?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Engineers report that underground tanks can capture roof runoff and fit beneath patios. Rainwater-collection systems can reduce stormwater runoff, and that supports this report. That report is also why tanks can be installed beneath patios in many new homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What about the ongoing administrative work?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Utility pilots show that stored rainwater cuts treated-water use and is inexpensive to monitor. That evidence supports lower household bills, supports the conclusion that rainwater collection reduces demand on mains water, and also shows that monitoring need not be costly.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you believe regulation can be kept simple?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: In other words, monitoring these systems is inexpensive enough to make compliance manageable. That is why simple monitoring makes the rule practical.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would you allow any flexibility in the design standard?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Put another way, patio-compatible tanks are a practical option for new homes. Therefore, the rules should permit that kind of installation rather than prescribe one exact design.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Terminally ill patients should have a legal right to request assisted dying, because a person's life and death belong to them.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Safeguards would never be enough to protect vulnerable patients. Legal assisted dying would pressure vulnerable patients into feeling like a burden.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Oregon has had its law since 1997, and its reports show that assisted deaths among vulnerable groups have not risen, which ignores your fear.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Those reports rely on doctors reporting on themselves, so they cannot reveal hidden coercion, and that is why the pressure is still a real worry.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: So you are saying we cannot trust the Oregon data.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Partly, yes. Doctors' prognoses are often wrong, since some patients given six months to live survive for years.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Palliative care cannot relieve all suffering, so some patients need the choice.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Most patients who ask for death change their minds once their pain is treated, so the choice is rarely needed.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: In other words, you think the choice is hardly needed, but a right matters even when few people use it.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Why should it matter if so few use it?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Because rights exist to protect minorities.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Put another way, a right protects even a single person, and I will grant that. My grandmother spent her last month in a hospice.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether youth football leagues should prohibit heading until players reach sixteen. Leopold supports the proposal, while Renata opposes it.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Youth football leagues should prohibit heading the ball until players reach sixteen. Repeated impacts before sixteen may expose young players to avoidable brain injury, which is why I support the ban.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: A nationwide age rule would give leagues a simple safety standard to enforce, which is another reason to adopt the ban.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Medical researchers still have unanswered questions about the long-term effects of heading during childhood, and that uncertainty is another reason to be cautious. Waiting until sixteen would reduce young players' exposure to repeated heading, so it is another reason to adopt the ban.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Coaches can teach passing, positioning, and defensive movement without requiring children to head the ball, so the ban is practicable. However, players need to practise heading before turning sixteen if they are expected to use the skill safely later.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: In other words, Leopold is advocating a complete ban on heading in youth football until players turn sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Leopold's proposal is to postpone heading rather than remove the skill from football permanently, so it supports prohibiting heading until players reach sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: The national youth finals are scheduled for a Saturday this season, incidentally.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: I began playing organised football at seven, but my own experience does not settle the medical question.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: We have heard the safety case, the training objection, and the argument that a clear age limit would be workable. The audience can now decide whether protecting developing players outweighs the loss of early heading practice.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether annual bonuses should depend more on team performance than on individual targets. Petra, could you start?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Team projects often depend on colleagues handing work from one stage to another. Because of that interdependence, I think bonuses should give more weight to team performance.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Individual targets can be gamed when employees contribute to shared work, so they should not dominate the bonus calculation.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Clients usually experience the work of a whole team rather than the output of one employee, which supports shifting the emphasis toward team results.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Then my proposal is that annual bonuses should give more weight to team performance than to individual targets.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: But a team-heavy formula could weaken accountability for individual results, so I would not approve an immediate permanent change.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The company has not yet gathered dependable evidence about whether team-based bonuses improve collaboration. That uncertainty is why I favour a measured approach.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: A six-month pilot would show whether a larger team component changes employee behaviour, which supports testing it first.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Publishing the bonus formula during the pilot would let employees understand how their contribution is assessed; that is another reason to run a transparent test.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Then the committee should test a team-weighted bonus formula before adopting it permanently.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: So you are saying that we should pilot the team-weighted formula before making a permanent change.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: There is a fairness issue, though: a team-weighted bonus could penalise specialists whose work supports projects without being visible in team results.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Role-adjusted measures could recognise behind-the-scenes contributions to team performance, which is why they belong in the design.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: The annual budget review is scheduled for Friday.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: For that reason, a team-weighted scheme should include role-adjusted measures for different kinds of work.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: In other words, the scheme needs different standards for visible project delivery and supporting work.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Individual targets can motivate employees to meet their own responsibilities, so they should remain part of the formula.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: An appeals process could protect employees when team results suffer for reasons outside their control; that supports keeping an individual element.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: The payroll vendor's contract is due for renewal in June.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: My recommendation is that the final scheme retain an individual-performance element while making team performance the larger component.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Put another way, the company should reward collective results more heavily without abandoning individual accountability.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Leilani, why do you support the change?

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Parents need information about a student's progress that they can talk over with teachers. A report card often gives results without providing a conversation.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: That need is why conferences are useful: twice-yearly meetings give parents a direct opportunity to ask questions about a student's progress.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Because parents need more than scores, teacher explanations during conferences can help them understand a student's difficulties.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: But parents do not need direct discussions with teachers because written report cards are sufficient. Meetings could also create an unnecessary burden for families.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: So you are saying that parents need progress information they can discuss directly with teachers.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Exactly, and for that reason schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Weekday evening parent events may still conflict with some families' schedules.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: I attended a parent-teacher meeting at my daughter's school last month. Amir, what would the proposed system mean for families who cannot attend?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: That is the central practical concern. We will now take questions about access and scheduling.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether councils should let residents vote directly on a fixed slice of the annual budget. Felix, you are in favour.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Yes, they should. Residents know better than officials which problems matter on their own streets, like broken lighting and potholes, and that is why the vote belongs to them.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Saanvi, is there evidence it works?

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: It raises turnout in civic life. In Felix's borough the scheme drew three times as many voters as the last by-election, so people clearly engage.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Sipho, you are sceptical.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: I am. People would back popular projects over necessary but dull maintenance, so this is a bad idea. I did sit on a parish council for years.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Felix, respond.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: But that ignores how it works, because officers shortlist the ballot first. They can screen out anything unaffordable or unlawful before it reaches voters.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Saanvi, anything on legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Direct votes make decisions more legitimate, since residents who help decide how money is spent are more willing to accept the outcome.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: So, Saanvi, in other words giving residents a direct vote would make people trust the council more.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: From the floor: the council would also save on the cost of complaints and appeals.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether managers should advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally. Bongani, make the case for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Internal candidates already understand the organisation's systems and culture. More importantly, employees deserve fair notice of opportunities to advance within their organisation.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: External recruitment can bring skills that the organisation does not currently possess. Some specialist vacancies also attract very few qualified internal applicants.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Rosalind raises the concern about restricting the search. Yusuf, what would an internal advertisement achieve?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Transparent internal advertising increases employees' trust in management. Employees are also more likely to apply for advancement when opportunities are clearly advertised.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Internal candidates often require less organisational induction than external hires, which can make the appointment more efficient.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Let us now consider the overall requirement.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: For those reasons, especially fair notice, greater trust, and wider participation, managers should be required to advertise vacancies internally before recruiting externally. The external applicants should still remain eligible after that internal advertisement.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: That sounds like a sequence rather than a ban on outside applicants. Yusuf, can the process remain practical?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Yes, because an internal-first rule would preserve access to external talent. A short internal application window would also prevent the recruitment process from becoming unnecessarily slow.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So the proposed safeguard is a brief internal window, followed by a normal comparison of candidates?

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Exactly. Managers could compare internal and external applicants after the internal advertisement period. This restates the earlier point that external applicants should remain eligible after an internal advertisement has been made. In other words, the proposal would open the door internally without shutting out outsiders.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So, in summary, the proposal is a mandatory internal advertisement before any external search. Put another way, employees would receive fair notice before managers looked outside the organisation.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: That is to say, the rule would preserve a fair chance for external applicants after internal notice. Separately, the company currently has twelve departments with separate recruitment budgets.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: But a mandatory internal stage could delay urgent recruitment by at least a week, so I would oppose an inflexible requirement.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The disagreement is therefore about timing, not whether internal employees deserve visibility. We will move to closing statements.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether managers should advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally. Bongani, make the case for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Internal candidates do not necessarily understand the organisation's systems and culture. More importantly, employees deserve fair notice of opportunities to advance within their organisation.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: External recruitment can bring skills that the organisation does not currently possess. Some specialist vacancies also attract very few qualified internal applicants.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Rosalind raises the concern about restricting the search. Yusuf, what would an internal advertisement achieve?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Transparent internal advertising increases employees' trust in management. Employees are also more likely to apply for advancement when opportunities are clearly advertised.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Internal candidates often require less organisational induction than external hires, which can make the appointment more efficient.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: For those reasons, especially fair notice, greater trust, wider participation, and lower induction costs, managers should be required to advertise vacancies internally before recruiting externally. The external applicants should still remain eligible after that internal advertisement.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: That sounds like a sequence rather than a ban on outside applicants. Yusuf, can the process remain practical?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Yes, because an internal-first rule would preserve access to external talent. A short internal application window would also prevent the recruitment process from becoming unnecessarily slow.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So the proposed safeguard is a brief internal window, followed by a normal comparison of candidates?

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Once the internal advertising period ends, managers could assess internal and external applicants together, thereby supporting the continued eligibility of external applicants. In other words, the proposal would open the door internally without shutting out outsiders.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So, in summary, the proposal is a mandatory internal advertisement before any external search. Put another way, employees would receive fair notice before managers looked outside the organisation.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: That is to say, the rule would preserve a fair chance for external applicants after internal notice. Separately, the company currently has twelve departments with separate recruitment budgets.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: But a mandatory internal stage could delay urgent recruitment by at least a week, so I would oppose an inflexible requirement.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The disagreement is therefore about timing, not whether internal employees deserve visibility. We will move to closing statements.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether mobile operating systems should be forced to allow alternative app stores. Rashid, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Platform owners take up to thirty percent commission on every sale, so they should be required to allow alternative stores.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: But a single curated store protects users better.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Damien, you look unconvinced. Open platforms see far more malware infections than closed ones, as the figures show.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Put another way, Ulla, you think only one gatekeeper can keep people safe. But that ignores independent scanners, which can vet apps from any source.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Rival stores would charge developers far less commission, so app prices would fall for consumers, and that is another reason to require them.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Rashid, your reaction?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put another way, Ifeoma, competition between stores would save consumers money.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Refunds and support get harder across many stores, which is another reason one store protects users better.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Damien, what about developers?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Small studios would reinvest their fee savings in new products, because they make most of the novel apps.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Ulla, can you sum that up?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: In other words, Damien, you think rivalry between stores would bring new apps.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Ifeoma, anything on safety?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Desktop computers have long let users sideload apps from third-party vendors without any approval step, so openness is workable on phones too.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Damien?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: So you are saying, Ifeoma, that phones should work like desktop computers.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Rashid, last word.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That is to say, desktop computers show that openness works.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Thank you all; a lively split tonight.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: I think amateur boxing should replace winning by knockout with points-only scoring. The aim should be to test skill without making one blow decisive.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would reduce the risk of serious head injuries, which is the strongest reason for the change.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Most amateur boxers have limited defensive experience because they are still developing their technique.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would also make bouts fairer when one lucky punch decides the result. That matters because a single dramatic moment can erase several rounds of better boxing.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: A single punch can end a bout even when the other boxer has performed better overall.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Another benefit is that points-only scoring would encourage boxers to develop a wider range of skills.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: They would gain more from footwork, defence, and sustained combinations if judges scored the whole performance, so training would become less focused on finding one big punch.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would make bouts less frightening for beginners, and that could help small clubs attract people.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Because points-only scoring would make bouts less frightening for beginners, beginners may leave boxing when they see a teammate lose by a sudden knockout.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Exactly, and points-only scoring would make it easier for clubs to retain new participants.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: But removing knockout victories would make boxing less honest about the sport's physical risks. A knockout is dangerous, but it also makes that danger impossible to ignore.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: So you are saying that a points-only system would conceal rather than solve boxing's dangers.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Put another way, Chloe's proposal would judge amateur boxers only on accumulated points instead of allowing a knockout to decide the bout.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Even so, points-only scoring would encourage a more patient style of amateur boxing.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: I have competed in three tournaments this year, although that experience does not settle the policy question.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Constance's concern, as I understand it, is that a points-only system could hide the seriousness of a hard punch.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: That concern is manageable because judges could still reward controlled pressure and accurate combinations under a points-only system.

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether pharmacies should be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment. Harriet, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Pharmacists receive training that enables them to recognise common minor infections. Because of that training, pharmacies should be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: That training means pharmacists can assess many routine infection cases without a doctor's appointment.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Pharmacies should be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment. A prescribing protocol could require pharmacists to refer patients with warning signs to doctors, so that safeguard is another reason to allow the policy.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: But some apparently minor infections are serious enough that uncertainty makes pharmacy prescribing unsafe, so that is a reason not to grant pharmacies this power.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether managers should advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally. Bongani, make the case for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Internal candidates already understand the organisation's systems and culture. More importantly, employees deserve fair notice of opportunities to advance within their organisation.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: External recruitment can bring skills that the organisation does not currently possess. Some specialist vacancies also attract very few qualified internal applicants.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Rosalind raises the concern about restricting the search. Yusuf, what would an internal advertisement achieve?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Transparent internal advertising increases employees' trust in management. Employees are also more likely to apply for advancement when opportunities are clearly advertised.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Internal candidates often require less organisational induction than external hires, which can make the appointment more efficient.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: For those reasons, especially fair notice, greater trust, wider participation, and lower induction costs, managers should be required to advertise vacancies internally before recruiting externally. The external applicants should still remain eligible after that internal advertisement.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: That sounds like a sequence rather than a ban on outside applicants. Yusuf, can the process remain practical?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Yes, because an internal-first rule would preserve access to external talent, external applicants should remain eligible; that preserved access also argues against requiring managers to advertise internally before recruiting externally. A short internal application window would also prevent the recruitment process from becoming unnecessarily slow, supporting continued eligibility for external applicants.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So the proposed safeguard is a brief internal window, followed by a normal comparison of candidates?

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Exactly. Managers could compare internal and external applicants after the internal advertisement period. In other words, the proposal would open the door internally without shutting out outsiders.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So, in summary, the proposal is a mandatory internal advertisement before any external search. Put another way, employees would receive fair notice before managers looked outside the organisation.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: That is to say, the rule would preserve a fair chance for external applicants after internal notice. Separately, the company currently has twelve departments with separate recruitment budgets.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: But a mandatory internal stage could hold up urgent recruitment for at least a week, so I would oppose an inflexible requirement.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The disagreement is therefore about timing, not whether internal employees deserve visibility. We will move to closing statements.
